Name: Requirements Gathering
Key Signals: Clarifies user workflows and scope; states workload and data freshness assumptions; agrees measurable latency and availability goals plus budget and timeline
Common Mistakes: Chooses architecture before requirements; treats guessed scale as observed traffic; specifies targets without a measurement window
Evaluation Criteria: Are requirements testable? Are assumptions explicit and revisited when constraints change? Is scope achievable within the budget?

Name: Back-of-Envelope Estimation
Key Signals: Derives average QPS from active users and requests per user; separates peak assumptions from averages; estimates retention and replication and index overhead with units
Common Mistakes: Equates DAU with QPS; treats illustrative hardware throughput as a benchmark; ignores workload skew and uncertainty
Evaluation Criteria: Do dimensions and arithmetic agree? Which assumptions dominate capacity? What representative measurements would confirm or disprove the estimate?

Name: High-Level Architecture
Key Signals: Starts with the simplest feasible design; traces request and data flows; assigns component responsibilities and explains failure boundaries
Common Mistakes: Adds queues or microservices or separate read/write services by default; draws boxes without data flow; ignores single points of failure relative to availability goals
Evaluation Criteria: Does the design satisfy stated requirements? Is each added component justified by a constraint? Are remaining failure risks explicit?

Name: Database Schema Design
Key Signals: Models entities and invariants alongside query patterns; specifies keys and applicable constraints; weighs index and denormalization costs
Common Mistakes: Assumes read-heavy workloads require denormalization; relies on application checks without concurrency reasoning; assumes foreign keys automatically index referencing columns
Evaluation Criteria: Can the schema preserve required invariants? Do indexes support actual queries without unjustified overhead? How are duplicated values kept consistent?

Name: API Design
Key Signals: Defines request and response contracts for chosen REST or RPC style; bounds collection responses with pagination; considers authorization and source/wire/behavioral compatibility
Common Mistakes: Treats page tokens as authorization; adds pagination after clients rely on full results; assumes additive fields or changed defaults cannot break clients
Evaluation Criteria: Are page limits and continuation behavior explicit? Are errors actionable? Can existing clients continue to work after the proposed change?

Name: Scaling Discussion
Key Signals: Identifies resource bottlenecks and uneven load; compares optimization and vertical or horizontal scaling as needed; accounts for failover capacity and partitioning costs
Common Mistakes: Assumes horizontal scaling is always necessary or linear; adds caches or shards without evidence; ignores hot keys and cross-partition operations
Evaluation Criteria: Does the proposal fit peak and failure workloads? What measurement triggers the next scaling step? Are skew and coordination costs addressed?

Name: Trade-off Analysis
Key Signals: Compares viable alternatives against explicit requirements; explains costs and failure consequences; revisits choices when assumptions change
Common Mistakes: Presents one architecture as universally correct; lists alternatives without decision criteria; confuses illustrative estimates with measured performance
Evaluation Criteria: Why does this option fit better under stated assumptions? What evidence would change the decision? Is added operational complexity justified?

Name: Failure Mode Analysis
Key Signals: Traces partial failures and overload propagation; budgets deadlines and bounded retries with backoff and jitter; plans load shedding and tests degraded operation
Common Mistakes: Treats timeouts as proof no side effect occurred; retries at every layer; assumes circuit breakers or failover always improve availability
Evaluation Criteria: What happens when a dependency is slow or never responds? Are retries safe and bounded? Can remaining capacity absorb failover traffic and recover after overload?

Name: Consistency vs Availability
Key Signals: States invariants and observable consistency guarantees per operation; explains CAP choices during partitions and PACELC latency tradeoffs without partitions; plans conflict recovery
Common Mistakes: Uses CAP as unconditional pick-two; confuses replica consistency with ACID constraint validity; assumes mixed consistency models are mandatory
Evaluation Criteria: Which operations can proceed during a partition without violating invariants? What staleness or rejected operations can users tolerate? Is one model sufficient or are multiple models justified?

Name: Operational Concerns
Key Signals: Connects user-facing SLIs and SLOs to actionable alerts; measures latency distributions and saturation; plans deployment evaluation and incident ownership
Common Mistakes: Mentions monitoring without a response plan; hides tail latency behind averages; assumes a canary proves safety despite shared dependencies or unrepresentative traffic
Evaluation Criteria: What symptom triggers action and who responds? Which signals stop or roll back a release? Can operators diagnose faults using telemetry and runbooks?

Name: Cost Awareness
Key Signals: Connects spending to business value and workload units; states usage and pricing assumptions; considers operating effort alongside infrastructure costs
Common Mistakes: Equates lowest bill with best design; presents estimates as quotes; ignores data transfer or reliability and staffing costs
Evaluation Criteria: Which cost drivers dominate at expected usage? Are price region and date assumptions explicit? Do savings preserve required service outcomes?

Name: Communication and Structure
Key Signals: Explains relevant past actions or proposed reasoning clearly; distinguishes personal contribution from team outcomes; answers follow-up questions with concrete evidence
Common Mistakes: Offers polished but unsupported claims; substitutes jargon for reasoning; treats a particular answer template as proof of competence
Evaluation Criteria: Is evidence relevant to the job competency? Can the reasoning and outcome be understood? Are candidates assessed with consistent questions and rating standards rather than presentation style alone?

Name: Idempotency and Ambiguous Outcomes
Key Signals: Recognizes that a timeout leaves the remote outcome unknown; defines retry identity and deduplication scope and lifetime; reasons about concurrent duplicates and external side effects
Common Mistakes: Generates a new key on every retry; assumes keys deduplicate forever; claims end-to-end exactly-once effects without defining the boundary
Evaluation Criteria: What happens if the response is lost after commit? How are repeated keys with different parameters handled? What happens after key expiry or a concurrent duplicate?

Name: Threat Modeling and Trust Boundaries
Key Signals: Identifies protected data and trust boundaries in the data flow; prioritizes plausible threats; maps authorization and other mitigations to testable requirements
Common Mistakes: Adds authentication without reasoning about authorization; assumes internal traffic is inherently trusted; lists controls without threats or residual risks
Evaluation Criteria: Which principal may perform each sensitive operation? What abuse crosses a trust boundary? How will mitigations be tested and remaining risk accepted?

Name: Recovery Objectives and Restore Validation
Key Signals: Defines acceptable downtime RTO and data loss RPO from business needs; compares recovery strategies and costs; plans backup restoration and failover/failback drills
Common Mistakes: Equates replication with protection from corruption; prescribes multi-region active-active for every workload; quotes recovery targets without testing dependencies and capacity
Evaluation Criteria: Can the whole workload recover to the required state within its time budget? Are backups usable after corruption? What evidence from recovery drills validates the design?
